generated_description.contextual_insights: The chart, produced by Our World in Data, displays historical national accounts estimates of the share of the world's population living on less than $5 per day, broken down by region from 1820 to 2017 [DIRECT]. The data is sourced from the Maddison Project Database, van Zanden et al., and de la Escosura (2020) [DIRECT]. The chart notes that because national accounts-based average incomes are typically higher than survey-based incomes, these poverty rates are lower than official World Bank estimates used to monitor Sustainable Development Goal 1 (SDG1) [DIRECT].
generated_description.domain_specific_explanations: In development economics, measuring poverty through national accounts (macroeconomic data) rather than household surveys often results in lower poverty estimates because national accounts capture broader economic activities that surveys might miss [SPECULATIVE: Development Economics]. The $5 per day threshold represents a moderate poverty line, which is higher than the international extreme poverty line [SPECULATIVE: Development Economics]. Visually, the chart shows that the global share of people living under this threshold has plummeted from approximately 87% in 1820 to about 15% in 2017 [DERIVED: reading and comparing the top boundary of the stacked area chart in 1820 and 2017].
generated_description.real_world_significance: This long-term trend highlights a profound global shift: over two centuries, poverty transitioned from being the default human condition to a minority state [SPECULATIVE: Economic History]. The regional breakdown reveals a dramatic shift in where the global poor reside; in 1820, large populations in China and India made up the bulk of those living under $5/day, whereas by 2017, Sub-Saharan Africa's share of the global poor expanded significantly relative to other regions [DERIVED: comparing the relative thickness of the regional bands between 1820 and 2017]. China's rapid industrialization and economic reforms starting in the late 20th century played a massive role in the steep decline of global poverty rates during that period [SPECULATIVE: Global Economic History]. This data is crucial for international development agencies to allocate resources and design policies targeting the remaining pockets of deep poverty, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa [SPECULATIVE: Development Policy].
